accuracy.evidence: Checked against NOAA Ocean Exploration 'How deep is the ocean?' (average depth 3,682 m; Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench 10,935 m, from the 2021 Deep-Sea Research I estimate; other surveys give up to 10,994 m, so the kid text says 'about 11,000 m'), the 2020 China–Nepal survey height of Everest (8,849 m, so 10,935 − 8,849 = 2,086 m of water above it, matching NOAA's 'over a mile'), NOAA 'What is the mid-ocean ridge?' (about 65,000 km, longest mountain range), USGS on Hawaiian shield volcanoes (Mauna Kea over 10,000 m from its sea-floor base) and Seabed 2030 (27.3% mapped to modern standards in 2025, 'about a quarter'). Echo times use about 1,500 m/s in sea water, so time = 2d ÷ 1500 (14.6 s for 10,935 m). Shelf under about 200 m and abyssal plains 3,000–6,000 m deep follow NOAA/Britannica. Parameterised answers checked at range corners: p2 b·1000 − a·100 (2,100..4,500), p4 a + b, m4 d − h (2..8), m7 d.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented alternative ideas for this age (Smithsonian Ocean and NOAA education notes; children's drawings of the sea floor as a flat 'bath'): the floor is flat (step 1 prediction, challenge 'flat', p1), the deepest water is in the middle of the ocean (step 2 prediction, probing the ridge gives 'Only 2,900 m… not the deepest part', tag 'middle'), the longest mountain range is on land (step 3 prediction), Everest would stick out of the trench (step 4 prediction, tags 'stick'/'fill', m1), islands float (step 5 prediction, tag 'float', m5), and a slow echo means shallow water (tags 'echo'/'fish', p5).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagseabed is built on this topic's own mechanisms: an echo sounder that plots depth from echo time onto a hidden bathymetric profile (shelf, seamount, abyssal plain, ridge with rift, trench), a depth probe that compares the middle ridge with the edge trench, Everest lowered on a true vertical scale into a 10,935 m trench, and a volcano that grows 1,000 m per eruption until it breaks the surface. flagdepth is about light zones, flagocean about shore/shallow/deep and flagland about land shapes seen from above; the 6-shingle gate passes against every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child discovers before being told: the floor stays hidden until 8 pings plot it, so 'not flat' comes from their own dots; the readout turns echo seconds into metres ('Echo 14.6 s → 10,935 m deep'); probing the middle shows the ridge is shallower than the trench; each '?' becomes a named feature with one line on what it is; the 'Top of Everest' counter goes from metres above the sea to '2,086 m under water'; the volcano readout flips from 'under water' to 'above the sea' as the island appears. Each task ends with the one-line idea.

predictions.evidence: Five predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab disproves: 'Flat, like the bottom of a bath' (the pings reveal mountains and a trench), 'Right in the middle' (the middle is a ridge at about 2,900 m), 'On land' (the mid-ocean ridge label gives 65,000 km under the sea), 'stick out of the sea' (Everest ends 2,086 m under water) and 'floating on the water' (the island is the top of a 5,000 m volcano standing on the floor).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Twelve wrong-answer messages, each naming the slip: 'flat' and 'hole' (the pings showed mountains, a plain and a trench), 'middle' (the middle often has a ridge), 'pole' (the Arctic is shallow by comparison), 'stick' and 'fill' (8,849 m against about 10,900 m), 'echo' and 'fish' (a long wait means the floor is far away), 'trench' and 'wave' (a ridge is raised solid floor), 'float' and 'sand' (islands are volcano tops made of rock).

readability.evidence: validate_lessons passes: family kid text FK 2.6 (limit 5.0) and adult FK 7.7 (limit 10). Kid sentences are short and concrete (bounces, long wait, piles up, pokes); curriculum words are kept and explained where they appear: ocean floor, trench, mid-ocean ridge, volcano, echo. Canvas text is 13–18 px dark ink on white pills; buttons say what they do (Move on and ping, Probe left, Name the next one, Lower Everest 2,000 m, Erupt!).

no_filler.evidence: Content gate passes (no banned phrases, explanation overlap under 12%). Kid paragraphs: how we know the depth (echo); shelf, plains and mountains; trench and the Everest comparison with numbers; volcano islands. Adult paragraphs: named features with depths and the NOAA average; seamounts, ridges, trench formation and the Challenger Deep figure; named common mistakes; echo sounding, mapping coverage and what the lab does.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots on iPhone 13 (390 px) in light and dark themes after Show me on all 6 steps. The first pass had the volcano spreading across the whole canvas, the volcano readout clipped at 390 px, and the 'Continental shelf' and 'Seamount' labels overlapping; the cone width is now capped, the readout is 'Top: 1,000 m above the sea', and the seamount label sits under its peak. The lab uses the young-learner button size and every tap target on the canvas (sea, floor, '?' markers, Everest, volcano) is large.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button: Move on and ping, Probe left / Probe right, Name the next one, Lower Everest 2,000 m, Erupt! (aria-labels name the action); the challenge uses buttons. say() updates the canvas aria-label and the visible live description after every ping, probe, name, lowering and eruption, with the numbers in words. walk.cjs (desktop and iPhone 13) completes all 5 tasks with Show me, shows the challenge, axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) is clean in both themes and there are no console errors.
